content: Palatal consonants are a specific category of consonantal sounds produced by raising the body of the tongue against the hard palate, which is the central part of the roof of the mouth. When the tip of the tongue is curled back towards the palate, these sounds are referred to as retroflex consonants. The most frequently occurring type of palatal consonant is the approximant [j] (as represented in the International Phonetic Alphabet, IPA). This sound is among the ten most common phonemes across the world's languages. Another common palatal consonant is the nasal [ɲ], which is present in approximately 35% of the world's languages. However, in most of these languages, the corresponding obstruent is not the plosive [c], but rather the affricate [t͡ʃ]. Languages that contrast palatal plosives with postalveolar affricates are relatively rare. Such contrasts are primarily found in a few languages spoken in northern Eurasia, the Americas, and central Africa. Notable examples include Hungarian, Czech, Slovak, and Albanian. It is important to note that the IPA symbols [c] and [ɟ] are often used not for true palatal stops, but instead for palatalized velar stops ([kʲ] and [gʲ]), palatal affricates ([c͡ç] and [ɟ͡ʝ]), alveolopalatal affricates ([t͡ɕ] and [d͡ʑ]), or even postalveolar affricates ([t͡ʃ] and [d͡ʒ]). This usage reflects an older tradition within the IPA. True palatal stops are relatively uncommon, so it is advisable to confirm the intended pronunciation whenever these symbols appear in the transcription of a language. Consonants with other primary places of articulation can also be palatalized. Palatalization involves the secondary articulation of raising the surface of the tongue towards the hard palate. For instance, the English sound [ʃ] (as in sh) has a palatal component, even though its primary articulation involves the tip of the tongue and the upper gum. This type of articulation is referred to as palatoalveolar. The International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) identifies specific palatal consonants, which are systematically categorized and studied in the field of phonetics.
